question: After Rome, which fats survive where — and what do cooks, monks, stewards and herders keep going?
summary: This is still a thin folio because the evidence thins, and because the library is stronger on later centuries; it has two dozen entries and says what each rests on. In the Latin north the Frankish estate rules tell stewards to account for fat, tallow, butter and soap ([[o1]]), monasteries and cathedrals keep an oil culture alive ([[b1]]), Anglo-Saxon butter is a lord’s luxury and Irish butter is buried in bogs ([[ec1]], [[ec2]]), and in Iceland families fight over stranded whales ([[c1]]). Soap is already a craft in Italy and Norsemen hunt whales and walrus ([[ec4]], [[ec5]]). Spain’s oil words come from Arabic ([[th1]]).

The Islamic world is the second centre. The Prophet is said to anoint himself with olive oil ([[b4]]); Baghdad’s tenth-century cookbook fries meat in sheep’s tail fat, rubs oven breads with sesame or unripe-olive oil and dresses cold dishes with olive oil, and its dietetic chapters weigh butter against clarified butter for the body ([[e1]], [[e2]], [[th2]]).

The east presses on. Tamil texts of the 600s–700s describe the sesame press, the *chekku*; Chola temples endow perpetual lamps with flocks of sheep to supply ghee ([[ec3]], [[b5]]); late-Tang calendars list pressing seeds for oil as a farm task, a monastery lamp is never allowed to go out, and the Tang pharmacopoeias rank milk, soured milk, su and ti hu as the stages of the soul ([[te1]], [[b2]], [[b3]]). The Tang table is the peak of Chinese dairy fat, with kaymak and ti-hu at banquets and fried sesame cakes sold on street corners by Iranians ([[ec8]], [[ec9]], [[e4]]). Japan goes the other way: Emperor Temmu bans meat eating in 675, cooking is done without oil or fat, and only a dairy tribute reaches the court ([[o2]], [[e3]], [[ec6]]). In Africa a village in Burkina Faso leaves a continuous record of shea-nut use from about 100 to 1500 AD ([[ec7]]).

themes.title: Oil in the northern fat world
text: Olive oil is carried across the break by the church, by Italian soap-makers and by Arabic, which gives Spain its words for oil; the Frankish estates show the animal-fat economy they sit in.

themes.title: Butter and whales at the Atlantic edge
text: Sheep’s butter as a thane’s luxury, bog butter, and the carcass disputes and whale hunts that precede the Basque industry.

themes.title: Baghdad’s kitchen and body
text: The tenth-century cookbook’s fats in the pot, on the oven wall and in the humoral chapters, and the Prophet’s oil.

themes.title: Asia presses and lights
text: The Tamil press, the Tang calendar, the Buddhist ladder and the lamps of Tang monasteries and Chola temples show fat as commodity and as offering; Tang dairy peaks while Japan’s court does without oil.

themes.title: Africa’s own fat: shea
text: The only African entry of the folio, and a reminder that the continent had a tree butter of its own long before the palm-oil trade.

themes.title: Japan without herds
text: Temmu’s meat ban, a diet with no oil or fat in the pot, and a milk-skin tribute: Ishige’s account of why animal fat never entered Japanese cooking.

turning_points.text: Dairy fats reach their peak in China under the part-Turkic Tang.
Monasteries keep an oil culture alive in the north.
The Tamil chekku presses sesame oil.
Emperor Temmu bans meat eating in Japan.
The Tang pharmacopoeia ranks milk, lo, su and ti hu as the stages of the soul.
Frankish estate stewards must account for fat, tallow and soap.
Sheep are given to feed perpetual temple lamps in the Chola country.
The Baghdad cookbook: tail fat in the pot, olive oil on the cold dishes.

how_to_read: Twenty-four entries, so read straight through. The *picture by region* counts the 24 entries: Europe 8, Near East 4, Far East 11, Africa 1; none in Americas, Oceania or Worldwide. Several dates are ranges for ‘the early Middle Ages’ because the sources do not narrow them.
The next folio is where documents (customs, Lent rules, Geniza ledgers, whale taxes) make fats countable.

sources.intro: A thin and uneven record: a translated Baghdad cookbook, a translated Frankish extract, South Indian inscriptions, a popular history of butter, Achaya, Needham, Anderson, Chang and Ishige for Asia, and Mueller, Ward and Ellis for Europe; three entries (Japan’s *so*, Spanish oil words, Kirikongo shea) rest on web summaries and one (the Prophet’s oil) on an unsourced anecdote.
main: Nasrallah’s translation of Ibn Sayyar for Baghdad ([[e1]], [[e2]], [[th2]]); the Fordham extract of the Capitulary De Villis ([[o1]]); South Indian Inscriptions vol. 23 ([[b5]]).

Needham and Kieschnick for the Tang entries ([[te1]], [[b2]], [[b3]]); Achaya for the Tamil press ([[ec3]]); Khosrova for butter ([[ec1]], [[ec2]]); Ward for soap ([[ec4]]); Ellis for whales ([[ec5]], [[c1]]).
Ishige for Japan ([[o2]], [[e3]]); Anderson and Chang (Schafer’s Tang chapter) for Tang dairy and the foreign cakes ([[ec8]], [[ec9]], [[e4]]).
contested: Mueller’s monastic ‘islands of oil’ cite no councils ([[b1]]); his anecdote of the Prophet’s oil names no source ([[b4]]).
The thousand-year-old Irish butter is a museum label as reported ([[ec2]]); the Icelandic sagas postdate the events ([[c1]]).
Spanish oil words show language, not the introduction of the crop ([[th1]]); the Kirikongo and *so* entries rest on abstracts and encyclopedia pages, not the papers ([[ec7]], [[ec6]]).
gaps: The Islamic agricultural writers are not covered: Watson’s *Agricultural Innovation in the Early Islamic World* (or an alternative) is not held, and Andalusian, Sicilian and Maghrebi (Ifriqiyan) olive oil are missing.

Africa has one entry; nothing on Aksum and Ethiopia’s butter and oilseeds, Nubia, the Sahel’s pastoral fats or the Swahili coast. Central Asia and the steppe, Tibet, Southeast Asia, the Americas (Maya, Andes) and the Pacific have no entry in these centuries; the search for them found no source in the library, and Reid’s book on Southeast Asia, now added, starts at 1450.

text: Eight entries, from the Frankish estates to the Irish bogs: the north’s fat is butter, tallow and soap, kept by stewards, hidden against raiders, fought over when a whale strands ([[o1]], [[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[c1]], [[ec5]]); the church and Arabic keep the Mediterranean’s oil in the picture ([[b1]], [[th1]], [[ec4]]).
Baghdad and the Prophet: cooking, dietetics and an oil anecdote ([[e1]], [[e2]], [[th2]], [[b4]]). The library holds the cookbook but not the Islamic agricultural writers.

The densest non-European record: the Tamil press and the Chola lamp-endowments, the Tang calendar, the monastery lamp, the Buddhist ladder, Tang kaymak, ti-hu and fried foreign cakes, and Japan, which bans meat in 675, cooks without oil and takes a milk-skin tribute ([[ec3]], [[b5]], [[te1]], [[b2]], [[b3]], [[ec9]], [[e4]], [[o2]], [[e3]], [[ec6]], [[ec8]]).

One entry: the shea record at Kirikongo, Burkina Faso ([[ec7]]). Africa’s fat history in these centuries is far larger than one entry; the library holds no source on Ethiopia, the Sahel’s herders, the Maghreb’s oil or the Swahili coast.
No entry. The search found nothing in the library on Maya, Andean or Arctic fats in 600–1000.
No entry. Pacific coconut voyages are in an earlier folio, with a placeholder date.
